igcse-0580-calc-enter-expressions.description: Copy the grouping of a written calculation into a scientific calculator and check the entry before finding its value.

sections.title: How do I keep a numerator and denominator together?
sections.label: Fraction template
sections.intro: Find the main fraction bar in the question. It divides all of the top expression by all of the bottom expression. Decide which numbers belong on each side before you type.

blocks.html: The fraction \(\dfrac{8+3}{9-4}\) has two grouped expressions. It is one division of the value on top by the value below.

figure.alt: A two-line calculator fraction template. The numerator occupies the whole top line and the denominator occupies the whole lower line.
figure.caption: Keep both whole expressions in the fraction template. The bar separates them.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Use a fraction template if your model has one. Enter the top, move to the bottom and enter it. For a one-line entry, put brackets around each whole part and put division between them.

blocks.title: Keep both parts of a fraction together
blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to find \(\frac{12+7}{10-4}\). Give the exact value.
blocks.hint: A fraction bar groups the whole numerator and the whole denominator.
blocks.solution:
Put \(12+7\) in the numerator and \(10-4\) in the denominator. With a division key, enclose both parts in brackets.

The calculator is dividing \(19\) by \(6\). The exact answer is \(\frac{19}{6}\).

retry.feedback: That result comes from dividing the middle numbers only. Put brackets around both whole parts.
The denominator contains a subtraction. Keep it together before dividing.

blocks.html: Typing a plus or minus after finishing a fraction changes which part it belongs to. Compare the expression on your screen with the original fraction bar.

blocks.title: Keep both parts of a fraction together
blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to find \(\frac{7+4}{13-3}\). Give the exact value.
blocks.hint: A fraction bar groups the whole numerator and the whole denominator.

The calculator is dividing \(11\) by \(10\). The exact answer is \(\frac{11}{10}\).

retry.feedback: That result comes from dividing the middle numbers only. Put brackets around both whole parts.
The denominator contains a subtraction. Keep it together before dividing.

sections.title: How far does the root extend?
sections.label: Root scope
sections.intro: A written root bar shows which expression the root covers. A calculator may draw a similar bar or put the root expression in brackets on one line.

blocks.html: Include every term beneath the bar in the same root. When you have copied all those terms, move the cursor out of the root or close its brackets.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Point to the first and last term under the written bar. Type those terms with their signs inside one root. Read the grouped entry back before evaluating.

blocks.title: Check where the square root ends
blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to work out \(\sqrt{100+44}\).
blocks.hint: Match the horizontal root bar in the question to the part of the screen inside the root.
blocks.solution:
Enter \(100+44\) inside one root template. In a one-line entry use brackets to put both terms inside the root.

The whole quantity under the root is \(144\). Its square root is \(12\).

retry.feedback: The addition is under the root bar. Your entry took the root of the first number only.

blocks.html: If you leave the root too early, later terms are added or subtracted after the root has been calculated.

blocks.title: Check where the square root ends
blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to work out \(\sqrt{25+24}\).
blocks.hint: Match the horizontal root bar in the question to the part of the screen inside the root.
blocks.solution:
Enter \(25+24\) inside one root template. In a one-line entry use brackets to put both terms inside the root.

The whole quantity under the root is \(49\). Its square root is \(7\).

retry.feedback: The addition is under the root bar. Your entry took the root of the first number only.

sections.title: When do I need brackets around a negative number?
sections.label: Negative number
sections.intro: A negative sign belongs to a number. Subtraction acts between two expressions. Some calculators use two different keys for those jobs.

blocks.html: In \((-6)^2\), the whole negative number is the base of the square. In \(-6^2\) the leading minus is outside the power.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Use the sign key or model equivalent to enter the negative number. Put brackets around the negative base before raising it to a power. Exit the power before typing the next operation.

blocks.title: Enter a negative base with brackets
blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to work out \((-7)^2+7\).
blocks.hint: Square the bracketed negative number before adding the final term.
blocks.solution:
Enter the negative sign and \(7\) within brackets before you press the square key. The base is \(-7\).

The square is \(49\). Move out of the exponent or close the brackets before adding \(7\). This gives \(56\).

retry.feedback: A leading minus outside brackets stays outside the square. The negative sign is part of the base here.
The final addition is outside the power. Exit the exponent before typing it.

blocks.html: A subtraction sign typed in place of a negative sign can give a syntax error or change the entry. Check both the sign and the brackets.

blocks.title: Enter a negative base with brackets
blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to work out \((-10)^2+3\).
blocks.hint: Square the bracketed negative number before adding the final term.
blocks.solution:
Enter the negative sign and \(10\) within brackets before you press the square key. The base is \(-10\).

The square is \(100\). Move out of the exponent or close the brackets before adding \(3\). This gives \(103\).

retry.feedback: A leading minus outside brackets stays outside the square. The negative sign is part of the base here.
The final addition is outside the power. Exit the exponent before typing it.

sections.title: Which version of the result should I keep?
sections.label: Exact or decimal
sections.intro: A calculator can sometimes show one result as a fraction and as a decimal. Read the answer instruction first. It tells you which form to record.

blocks.html: An exact fraction keeps the full value. A decimal display for a recurring fraction has a limited number of places and normally shows an approximation.

figure.alt: One stored calculator answer can be shown as a fraction or as a decimal.
figure.caption: The answer-format control changes the display of the stored value.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Use your model’s answer-format control to view a decimal when the question asks for one. Keep the exact fraction if the question asks for an exact answer. If the task asks for digits displayed, copy the display before rounding.

blocks.title: Choose the exact calculator result
blocks.prompt: The calculator can show \(\frac{23}{7}\) or the six-place display \(3.285714\). The question asks for an exact answer. Which result should you write?
blocks.hint: A result can have an exact fraction and a rounded decimal display.
blocks.solution:
The decimal form of this fraction continues. The six decimal places on the display omit later digits.

Use \(\frac{23}{7}\). It records the whole value exactly.

retry.feedback: The decimal is only the number shown to six places. Use the exact fraction.
Rounding again removes more digits. The question asks for the whole value.
Turning the fraction over changes the value. Read the exact fraction as shown.

blocks.html: A decimal approximation can look close to the fraction. If the question asks for the exact value, write the fraction or another exact form.

blocks.title: Choose the exact calculator result
blocks.prompt: The calculator can show \(\frac{12}{7}\) or the six-place display \(1.714286\). The question asks for an exact answer. Which result should you write?

sections.title: How do I change the display without changing the result?
sections.label: Convert the view
sections.intro: The exact-to-decimal control acts on the calculated answer. Its name varies between models. A calculator might label this control as Format or show a symbol for switching between fraction and decimal.

blocks.html: Changing how the answer is displayed keeps the stored value. Some calculators can also limit the number of decimal places they show, so inspect the display before copying it.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: If a fraction terminates as a decimal, choose the decimal display and read its digits. You can also divide the numerator by the denominator to find the decimal.

blocks.title: Switch a result to decimal form
blocks.prompt: Your calculator shows \(\frac{4}{40}\). Use its answer-format control or divide the numerator by the denominator. Give the exact decimal.
blocks.hint: A fraction is numerator divided by denominator. The decimal button changes the way it is shown.
blocks.solution:
Change the format of the stored fraction to decimal. The answer-format control may have a different name on your model.

The exact decimal is \(0.1\). Converting the display has kept the same value.

retry.feedback: Divide the numerator by the denominator in that order.

blocks.html: Use the numerator first. Reversing the division gives the reciprocal of the original answer.

blocks.title: Switch a result to decimal form
blocks.prompt: Your calculator shows \(\frac{7}{16}\). Use its answer-format control or divide the numerator by the denominator. Give the exact decimal.
blocks.hint: A fraction is numerator divided by denominator. The decimal button changes the way it is shown.
blocks.solution:

The exact decimal is \(0.4375\). Converting the display has kept the same value.

retry.feedback: Divide the numerator by the denominator in that order.

sections.title: What setting matches an angle in degrees?
sections.label: Degrees indicator
sections.intro: The unit next to an angle in the question tells you how to enter it for a trigonometric calculation. Check the indicator on your calculator before you type a degree angle.

blocks.html: Use degrees when the question uses degrees. The indicator may say DEG or D. RAD or R indicates radians.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Look up the angle setting on your model. Choose the unit given in the question, then check the indicator on the screen. Angle setting and decimal format are separate controls.

blocks.title: Choose a setting for an angle in degrees
blocks.prompt: The question includes the angle \(40^\circ\). Your calculator shows RAD. Which change makes the angle entry match the question?

options.A: Turn on a fixed number of decimal places.
options.C: Keep RAD and enter the same number.
options.D: Switch the answer from a fraction to a decimal.

blocks.hint: Match the angle mode to the unit printed next to the angle.
blocks.solution:
The degree sign beside \(40\) gives the unit. The calculator’s RAD setting expects angles measured in radians.

Change the angle unit to degrees and check the indicator. The keys or menus depend on the model.

retry.feedback: The calculator would read a value in radians. The degrees symbol in the question matters.
The answer format and the angle unit are separate settings.
A display precision setting does not change the angle unit.

blocks.html: Changing the display to a fraction or decimal leaves the angle unit alone. Check the angle indicator directly.

igcse-0580-calc-precision-and-checking.description: Use the full stored answer between steps, record the final result as requested, and catch a wrong-looking display.

sections.title: How can I keep all the digits between steps?
sections.label: Stored last answer
sections.intro: If a calculation has two stages, use the full first result in the next stage. Retyping a shortened display can change the final value even when all the operations are correct.

blocks.html: Enter the whole expression with the right grouping, or use the last-answer memory if your model has it. The label ANS is common.

figure.alt: Three stages. Keep all digits after the first step. Use the stored value in the next step. Round the final answer if requested.
figure.caption: Preserve the stored answer through every intermediate operation.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Write the expression you are calculating on paper. Use the exact stored result or the full grouped expression on the calculator. Round only the answer requested at the end.

blocks.title: Keep the stored value between steps
blocks.prompt: The first step is \(\frac{31}{8}\). Write down the result after multiplying that full value by \(12\). Give the exact value.
blocks.hint: Use the value already stored in the calculator. Rounding the first result can change the final answer.
blocks.solution:
The first result is \(3.875\). Carry the full value through by leaving the two steps in one expression or by using the stored last answer.

Multiply it by \(12\) to get \(46.5\).

retry.feedback: Your result matches retyping \(3.88\). Keep all digits of the first result until the final calculation.

blocks.html: Copying back a rounded result can spread the error to the next calculation. Use the stored answer before you change it.

blocks.title: Keep the stored value between steps
blocks.prompt: The first step is \(\frac{37}{8}\). Write down the result after multiplying that full value by \(4\). Give the exact value.
blocks.hint: Use the value already stored in the calculator. Rounding the first result can change the final answer.
blocks.solution:
The first result is \(4.625\). Carry the full value through by leaving the two steps in one expression or by using the stored last answer.

Multiply it by \(4\) to get \(18.5\).

retry.feedback: Your result matches retyping \(4.63\). Keep all digits of the first result until the final calculation.

sections.title: Which digits belong in the final answer?
sections.label: Final instruction
sections.intro: Look for the answer instruction before writing a number from the display. It may ask for an exact form, all the displayed digits or a stated precision.

blocks.html: Read the original unrounded result for your final rounding decision. If an earlier part asked for a rounded answer, use the full value again when a later part continues the calculation.

blocks.title: Try this method

sections.title: How can I check a result that looks wrong?
sections.label: Sense check
sections.intro: Before copying the answer, ask whether its sign and size are plausible. If possible, reverse an operation as a second check.

blocks.html: A positive number multiplied by a factor below one half must give less than half the original value. If you divided, multiply the quotient by the divisor to check that you recover the starting number.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Use a quick size or sign check first. If the result fails, inspect what you typed. Re-enter the calculation with the full brackets and use an inverse check when it is available.

blocks.title: Use a quick size check
blocks.prompt: You want to calculate \(25\times0.21\). The second factor is less than \(0.5\). Which displayed result is correct?
blocks.hint: Multiplying by a positive number less than one half gives less than half of the starting value.
blocks.solution:
The product must be less than half of \(25\), so it must be less than \(12.5\).

Re-enter the digits carefully. The exact product is \(5.25\).

retry.feedback: This is too large to be less than half the first factor. Check the decimal point you typed.
This is one tenth of the correct product. Re-enter the second factor as shown.
The expression asks for multiplication. Check the operation on your display.

blocks.html: Typing the same mistaken entry twice can repeat the same mistake. Use a different check, such as the inverse operation.

blocks.title: Check a quotient with the inverse operation
blocks.prompt: You calculated \(55\div 11=5\). Which check uses the result to confirm the original division?
blocks.hint: Use the opposite operation and check that you return to the original number.
blocks.solution:
Multiplication reverses division. It should return the number you started with.

Check that \(5\times 11=55\).

retry.feedback: Adding reverses subtraction. Multiplying reverses division.
Dividing again applies the original operation a second time.
Multiply the quotient by the divisor. The result should be the starting number.

revision.body:
How can I keep all the digits between steps?

Enter the whole expression with the right grouping, or use the last-answer memory if your model has it. The label ANS is common.

Write the expression you are calculating on paper. Use the exact stored result or the full grouped expression on the calculator. Round only the answer requested at the end.

Which digits belong in the final answer?

Read the original unrounded result for your final rounding decision. If an earlier part asked for a rounded answer, use the full value again when a later part continues the calculation.

Keep your full result on the screen until you have checked how many places the question requests. Apply the stated rounding rule once, at the end.

How can I check a result that looks wrong?

A positive number multiplied by a factor below one half must give less than half the original value. If you divided, multiply the quotient by the divisor to check that you recover the starting number.

Use a quick size or sign check first. If the result fails, inspect what you typed. Re-enter the calculation with the full brackets and use an inverse check when it is available.

igcse-0580-calc-money-and-time-display.description: Interpret decimal money and enter or read durations in decimal hours or a supported hours–minutes–seconds display.

sections.title: How do I write a decimal result as money?
sections.label: Money
sections.intro: Money in pounds and pence uses two places after the decimal point. A calculator can leave out a trailing zero even when that zero belongs in the written amount.

blocks.html: \(6.7\) pounds is £6.70. The decimal part is seven tenths of a pound, which is seventy pence.

figure.alt: A unit check branches to pounds and pence for money or hours and minutes for time.
figure.caption: Read the unit before deciding how to interpret the decimal part.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Read the whole pounds from before the point. Read the pence from the two places after it. Write the unit and use both pence digits.

blocks.title: Write the calculator result as money
blocks.prompt: The calculator shows \(3.9\) pounds. Which written amount correctly uses pounds and pence?
blocks.hint: A tenth of a pound is ten pence. Read both places after the decimal point.
blocks.solution:
The first digit after the point represents tenths of a pound. There are 90 pence in that part.

Write two digits for the pence, so \(3.9\) pounds is written £3.90.

retry.feedback: This reads the tenths digit as a single penny. Each tenth is ten pence.
The digits before the decimal point give the full pounds.
The display includes part of a pound. Keep the pence.

blocks.html: A tenths digit represents tens of pence. For example, £6.07 names seven pence and gives a different amount from £6.70.

blocks.title: Write the calculator result as money
blocks.prompt: The calculator shows \(6.6\) pounds. Which written amount correctly uses pounds and pence?
blocks.hint: A tenth of a pound is ten pence. Read both places after the decimal point.
blocks.solution:
The first digit after the point represents tenths of a pound. There are 60 pence in that part.

Write two digits for the pence, so \(6.6\) pounds is written £6.60.

retry.feedback: This reads the tenths digit as a single penny. Each tenth is ten pence.
The digits before the decimal point give the full pounds.
The display includes part of a pound. Keep the pence.

sections.title: How do decimal hours give minutes?
sections.label: Read decimal hours
sections.intro: The number before the decimal point is the number of whole hours. The digits after the point describe a fraction of the next hour.

blocks.html: In \(2.45\) hours, the fractional part is \(0.45\) hour. Multiply by 60 to get \(27\) minutes.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: Separate out the whole hours. Multiply the decimal part by 60 to find the remaining minutes. Check that the minutes are fewer than 60.

blocks.title: Read the minutes in a decimal-hour display
blocks.prompt: The calculator shows a duration of \(7.65\) hours. It contains 7 whole hours and some minutes. How many minutes remain after the 7 whole hours?
blocks.hint: The numbers after the point represent part of an hour. One hour has 60 minutes.
blocks.solution:
The decimal part is \(\frac{13}{20}\) of an hour.

Multiply that part by \(60\). The duration is 7 hours 39 minutes.

retry.feedback: The digits after the point count hundredths of an hour. Multiply that fraction by 60 to find minutes.

blocks.html: The digits to the right of the decimal point are parts of one hour. Copying them directly as minutes changes the duration.

blocks.title: Read the minutes in a decimal-hour display
blocks.prompt: The calculator shows a duration of \(2.75\) hours. It contains 2 whole hours and some minutes. How many minutes remain after the 2 whole hours?
blocks.hint: The numbers after the point represent part of an hour. One hour has 60 minutes.
blocks.solution:
The decimal part is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of an hour.

Multiply that part by \(60\). The duration is 2 hours 45 minutes.

retry.feedback: The digits after the point count hundredths of an hour. Multiply that fraction by 60 to find minutes.

sections.title: How do I enter hours and minutes correctly?
sections.label: Enter hours minutes
sections.intro: Check that all parts of the calculation need the same unit. If the entry is in hours, first convert the minutes to a fraction of an hour.

blocks.html: To enter 4 hours 36 minutes, use \(4+\dfrac{36}{60}=4.6\) hours. Some models also support a sexagesimal entry, shown as \(4^\circ\,36'\,0''\) in a time calculation.

blocks.title: Try this method
blocks.html: For decimal entry, divide minutes by 60 and add the whole hours. If you use a sexagesimal key, follow your model’s instructions and check whether the display is currently in decimal hours or hours, minutes and seconds.

blocks.title: Enter hours and minutes as a decimal
blocks.prompt: A calculation needs a duration of 2 hours 9 minutes in decimal hours. What number should you enter?
blocks.hint: Divide the minutes by 60 before adding them to the whole hours.
blocks.solution:
Write the minutes as \(\frac{9}{60}\) of an hour.

Add this to \(2\). Use \(2.15\) for the decimal-hour entry.

retry.feedback: Writing the minute digits after the point converts them into hundredths of an hour. Divide by 60 instead.

blocks.html: A sexagesimal display uses symbols that can also appear for angles. Read those three groups as time only when the calculation is about a duration.

blocks.title: Read a time entry from a sexagesimal display
blocks.prompt: On a calculator with a sexagesimal time entry, the display for a duration is \(2^\circ\,21'\,0''\). Write the duration in decimal hours.
blocks.hint: The same display symbols can occur for angles. The question tells you the context is time.
blocks.solution:
For a time calculation, the three groups represent hours, minutes and seconds. The display has 2 hours and 21 minutes, with no seconds.

Use \(2+\frac{21}{60}=2.35\) decimal hours.

retry.feedback: These are minutes. Divide them by 60 before including them in a decimal-hour value.

How do I write a decimal result as money?

\(6.7\) pounds is £6.70. The decimal part is seven tenths of a pound, which is seventy pence.

Read the whole pounds from before the point. Read the pence from the two places after it. Write the unit and use both pence digits.

How do decimal hours give minutes?

In \(2.45\) hours, the fractional part is \(0.45\) hour. Multiply by 60 to get \(27\) minutes.

Separate out the whole hours. Multiply the decimal part by 60 to find the remaining minutes. Check that the minutes are fewer than 60.

How do I enter hours and minutes correctly?

To enter 4 hours 36 minutes, use \(4+\dfrac{36}{60}=4.6\) hours. Some models also support a sexagesimal entry, shown as \(4^\circ\,36'\,0''\) in a time calculation.

For decimal entry, divide minutes by 60 and add the whole hours. If you use a sexagesimal key, follow your model’s instructions and check whether the display is currently in decimal hours or hours, minutes and seconds.
